clue.text: People on the American side likened to mad dogs

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it, so the people come after the side

parts.note: in American pool and billiards, side or spin put on the cue ball is called english
men is a common crossword synonym for people

explanation.surface: Someone compares the folk across the Atlantic to rabid dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls Noel Coward's song 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen', who go out in the midday sun. 'on' sets the people after the side; Americans call spin on a billiard ball english.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's famous song title pairs these countrymen with mad dogs, as both go out in the midday sun.

clue.text: Show up French revolutionary in German city

indicators.note: the revolutionary is placed inside the name of the German city

parts.note: Ems (Bad Ems) is a spa town in Germany
Paul Barras was a leader of the French Revolution and the Directory

explanation.surface: A French radical turns up in a German town and makes a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To show someone up is to make them feel awkward and ashamed in front of others.

clue.text: After 5, soldier is brave

indicators.note: the soldier comes after the word drawn from clue 5

parts.note: the answer to 5 down means irk, as does gall
an ant is a soldier in the insect world, a stock crossword equation

explanation.surface: Following some earlier event, a fighting man proves courageous.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' points to the answer of 5 down, used as a verb meaning irritate. 'After' puts the soldier behind its synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallant person is valiant and bold, so it is a straight synonym for courageous.

clue.text: I try cues out for peace of mind

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the fodder are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A snooker player experiments with cues to feel calmer about the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the eight letters of I TRY CUES.
explanation.definitionFit: Security is the state of feeling safe and free from worry, a synonym for peace of mind.

clue.text: Profit for little effort — as made by oakum pickers?

definitions.meaning: an idiom for easy gains got with hardly any work
oakum was loose fibre picked from old ropes, often by prisoners and workhouse inmates, so their earnings came literally from that rope

explanation.surface: Easy earnings, like those of the Victorian poor who unpicked rope for fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: Oakum picking was a menial Victorian task in British prisons and workhouses: unravelling old tarred rope into fibre for caulking ships.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes pay received for work that is trivial, and literally fits cash earned by unpicking used cordage.

clue.text: Bug revealed in weed

definitions.meaning: to bug someone is to irritate or annoy them
a stinging plant common as a garden weed

explanation.surface: An insect turns up in the weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like an insect noun but is the verb irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for irritate and the stinging plant regarded as a garden weed.

clue.text: Son has to get older, and wise

parts.note: to age is to grow older

explanation.surface: A boy must grow up and become sensible.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage as an adjective means showing deep wisdom and sound judgment.

clue.text: Old-fashioned communication in rhyme

parts.note: the slow postal service is named with two rhyming words, one a sluggish garden creature

explanation.surface: A letter written in verse, the way people used to correspond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in rhyme' suggests a poem, but means the two-word name rhymes with itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular term for letters sent by ordinary post, as against email, whose two halves rhyme.

clue.text: Monarch relaxed, being well lubricated V

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, stands for King George
eased means loosened or relaxed

explanation.surface: A king unwinds after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well lubricated' suggests drunk in the surface; in the answer it means oiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something greased has been coated with grease or oil, so it is thoroughly lubricated.

clue.text: Will preserve in a cylindrical pot

parts.note: Billy and Will are both short forms of William
to can food is to preserve it in a tin

explanation.surface: Someone decides to bottle food in a tin pot.
explanation.walkthrough: A billycan is the tin pot used for boiling water over a campfire in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: A billycan is a metal cooking pot shaped like a cylinder, used outdoors over a fire.

clue.text: Crater erupts — it produces a trail of light

definitions.text: it produces a trail of light

indicators.note: an eruption throws things about, so the letters of the word before are scattered

explanation.surface: A volcanic crater bursts and sends out a glowing streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erupts' rearranges CRATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracer bullet or shell burns as it flies, leaving a visible streak of light behind.

clue.text: Papers begin reporting every amateurish mistake

indicators.note: the words begin with the letters needed, so take each one's opening letter

explanation.surface: Newspapers start writing up every clumsy error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'begin' takes the first letters of 'reporting every amateurish mistake'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ream is a quantity of paper, conventionally 480 or 500 sheets.

clue.text: Two men get drunk in sequence

parts.note: Roy is a man's name
Al is a second man's name
flush is old slang for tipsy, flushed with drink

explanation.surface: A couple of blokes go out and get plastered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sequence' points to poker, where the top hand is the ace-high run in one suit.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker this hand is the ace-high run of five cards all in one suit, the best possible sequence.

clue.text: For coverage, move into a tent

indicators.note: the letters of the following words are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: Campers are told to shift into a tent for shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' rearranges INTO A TENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Media attention is the coverage given to a story by the press.

clue.text: "This could improve your appearance' DYE I say to dog

indicators.note: say signals the letter is pronounced, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the letter I sounds like the organ of sight
to dog someone is to follow or shadow them

explanation.surface: A make-up advert addressed oddly to a pet.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed is garbled by OCR; it reads 'This could improve your appearance - I say, to dog'. 'say' signals a sound-alike for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Eye make-up is cosmetics applied to the eyelids, worn to enhance the face.

clue.text: Raccoon-like animal seen in Japan daily

indicators.note: the animal can be seen inside the run of letters of the next words

explanation.surface: A creature that appears in a Japanese newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The red panda was long classed with raccoons, and the name covers it as well as the giant bear.

clue.text: Go in fear of arrest

definitions.meaning: to dread or anticipate something with anxiety
to take a suspect into custody

explanation.surface: Being afraid of getting nicked by the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to anticipate with dread and to seize a person for the law.

clue.text: Old horse has to make fast turn

definitions.meaning: a broken-down, worn-out horse is called this in old slang
to fasten something by turning it, as with a threaded fixing

explanation.surface: An ageing horse must spin round quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' reads as speedy, but means secure: you turn it to fix it fast.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old term for a worn-out nag and a verb for tightening by twisting.

clue.text: Gosh — indisposed? Get warm

clue.text: Strips off old item of clothing — backing appears to drop off

indicators.note: going backwards, so the run of letters built here is read in reverse

parts.note: peels means strips off a layer
a tog is a garment, as in togs for clothes

explanation.surface: Someone peels off an old garment that seems ready to fall away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' reverses PEELS + O + TOG, giving the whole answer at once.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is an idiom for nodding off into slumber.

clue.text: No longer around, but incorporated in revised text

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the rearranged word
a revised text has been altered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: Inc is the US abbreviation for incorporated

explanation.surface: A company's name is gone, though it appears in an edited document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' makes EXTT, a rearrangement of the clue's word text; 'in' puts the company abbreviation inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An extinct species or institution has died out and no longer exists.

clue.text: Threaten naughty child with death

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
end can mean death, as in meet one's end

explanation.surface: A parent warns a badly behaved child of dire consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: To impend is to loom or hang over as an imminent danger.

clue.text: Mathematician agreed with god outside

indicators.note: the god's name goes around the outside of the word for agreed

parts.note: Ares is the Greek god of war
chimed (in) means agreed or harmonised

explanation.surface: A mathematician who concurred with a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps the war god around the word for agreed, as in 'chimed in with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes of Syracuse was the great ancient Greek mathematician and inventor.

clue.text: Left out of shape by swelling

indicators.note: the letter for left is taken out of the word for shape

parts.note: style can mean form or shape

explanation.surface: Someone is disfigured by a swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out of' looks like one phrase: Left gives L, and 'out of' removes it from STYLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the edge of the eyelid.

clue.text: Glider crashed in historic zone

indicators.note: a crashed glider is wrecked, so its letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A glider comes down in a site of historical interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashed' rearranges GLIDER. Zone is an archaic word for a belt.
explanation.definitionFit: Zone once meant a belt worn round the waist, so a girdle is an old-fashioned zone.

clue.text: Guns, one out of order …

indicators.note: the letter for one is removed from the word for order

parts.note: an ordinance is an authoritative order or decree
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Guns drawn, one breaks ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to the next clue for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance is military artillery and weapons collectively, so it means guns.

clue.text: … killed a large number in America

definitions.meaning: American slang for a great quantity, as in a whole lot of something

explanation.surface: A gunman shot many people in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to the previous clue only for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the past tense of slay and an American informal noun for a great many.

clue.text: Set also seen about in crimson (4-6) 23,248 Solution

indicators.note: the turned word goes inside the shade of red

parts.note: deep red is a description of crimson

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: too means also

explanation.surface: A setting where crimson is seen as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the word for also into OOT; 'in' places that inside the shade of crimson. The trailing '23,248 Solution' in the held clue is page noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep-rooted beliefs are firmly established, set fast like a long-rooted plant.
